ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: An AI model proposes a new antibiotic that works in mice

explainer.found: An AI model proposed a new antibiotic that cleared a drug-resistant skin infection in 8 of 10 mice. The model, Halden Design, ranked about 12 million molecules. The team made and tested 40 of the top ones. Three of the 40 stopped the growth of drug-resistant bacteria in dishes.
explainer.matters: Antimicrobial resistance makes some infections hard to treat, and doctors need new antibiotics. A first safety trial of the compound in people is registered as NCT09999001. The trial plans to enrol 24 healthy volunteers. It tests safety, not cure.
explainer.ai_helped: Halden Research built Halden Design, which ranks molecules by their chance of killing drug-resistant bacteria. The model proposed which molecules to make. People made them and ran every test. The Coldwater Institute ran the mouse tests and runs the safety trial.
explainer.how_sure: Checked. Cell published the paper after peer review. Halden Research, which built the model, helped write the paper, and no other lab has repeated the tests. The Coldwater Institute says it ran the mouse tests and runs the first safety trial.
explainer.background: Drug makers once found antibiotics by testing natural samples one by one. Computers can now rank a huge list of molecules before anyone makes one. That lets labs test only the best candidates.
explainer.could_lead: If later trials go well, the compound could become a treatment for drug-resistant infections. It might also show that AI can find other new antibiotics. First, other labs must repeat the tests.

evidence.quote: Our model, Halden Design, ranked about 12 million molecules for their chance of killing drug-resistant bacteria

rung_history.note: A second lab with no tie to the first repeated the mouse tests.

since_then.text: A second lab, Kestrel College, repeated the mouse tests with its own mice and samples. The compound cleared the infection in 7 of 10 mice. The lab says it has no tie to Halden Research.

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: A research council plans to ask applicants about AI use

explainer.found: The Aldgate Research Council published a draft rule on AI in grant proposals. Applicants would have to say if AI tools helped write any part of a proposal. The draft asks for this statement in the proposal summary only. Comments are open until the end of the year.
explainer.matters: Research councils decide who receives funding. A rule on AI use tells applicants what they must disclose, and it tells reviewers what they are reading. Other funders could copy a rule like this one, so its wording may matter far beyond one council.
explainer.ai_helped: No AI system is named in the draft. The rule is about AI tools in general: it covers any tool that helped write a proposal. The council asks applicants to say what help they had, not which tool gave it.
explainer.how_sure: Claimed. The Aldgate Research Council states the draft in its own announcement. It is a proposal, not yet a rule, and the council may change it after the comment period closes. No other source we read says how the council will act.
explainer.background: Funding councils receive many proposals each year. Writers use many tools, from spell checkers to AI chatbots. A disclosure rule asks them to say what help they had.
explainer.could_lead: A final rule could set a pattern for other funders. It might also push applicants to hide their use of AI if the rule is unclear. Clear examples in the rule could prevent that.

evidence.quote: Applicants must say if AI tools helped write any part of a proposal

since_then.text: The council published its final rule. From 1 January, applicants must say if AI tools helped write any part of a proposal. The final rule covers every part of a proposal, not only the summary.

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: A robotic lab finds a cheap metal mixture that splits water

explainer.found: A robotic lab at Eastvale University tested 200 mixtures of common metals in six weeks. One mixture sped up the splitting of water into hydrogen almost as well as platinum does.
explainer.matters: Platinum is rare. A cheap mixture that works nearly as well could make hydrogen from water less costly.
explainer.ai_helped: Marlow Labs built Marlow Selector, which chose which mixtures to try next. Robot arms mixed and tested the samples.
explainer.how_sure: Checked. The Eastvale Journal of Materials published the paper. The tests ran in one lab, and Marlow Labs, the maker of the AI system, helped write it.
explainer.background: Splitting water gives hydrogen. The reaction needs a material that speeds it up, and platinum is a common choice.
explainer.could_lead: Robot labs could search many more mixtures in the same time and find other cheap materials.

evidence.quote: Marlow Selector, built by Marlow Labs, chose which mixtures to try next

rung_history.note: An independent lab repeated the work and got a matching result.

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: Tiles that fill a surface only without repeating

explainer.found: Two mathematicians at Eastvale University proved that tiles of one kind can fill a flat surface only in patterns that never repeat. Mathematicians had left this question open since 1968. The proof runs to 38 pages and needs no computer search. Other mathematicians can follow every step of it by hand, without special tools.
explainer.matters: Tilings appear in computer science and in the study of materials. A proof that some tiles can never form a repeating pattern tells designers what such patterns can and cannot do. It settles a question that had stood since 1968, and it gives researchers a new method to use.
explainer.how_sure: Checked. The Journal of Tiling Theory published the paper after peer review. Two mathematicians who were not on the paper, at Kestrel College and Northgate University, say they read the proof and found no gap. Their words are quoted on this page. The result stands on the journal's review and their reading, not on any claim by the authors.
explainer.background: A tiling covers a surface with copies of shapes and leaves no gaps. A floor of square tiles repeats the same pattern again and again. This proof is about tiles that can never do that.
explainer.could_lead: The method could help with the three-dimensional case, which is still open. It might also help scientists who study materials with patterns that never repeat, and designers who need such patterns in their work.

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: Reviewers shared unpublished papers with an AI chatbot

explainer.found: The journal eLife found that reviewers pasted the text of 31 unpublished manuscripts into a public AI chatbot to help write their reports.
explainer.matters: Authors send unpublished work to a journal in confidence. Pasting it into a public tool breaks that trust and may expose the work.
explainer.ai_helped: Reviewers used an AI chatbot to help write reports. eLife does not name the chatbot.
explainer.how_sure: Checked. eLife, the journal involved, says so in its own statement and in an editorial note.
explainer.background: Peer review is the step where outside experts judge a paper before it is published.
explainer.could_lead: Journals could write clear rules and tell reviewers what they may share.

evidence.quote: pasted the text of 31 unpublished manuscripts into a public AI chatbot

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: An AI model forecasts the weather ten days ahead

explainer.found: Larch Weather Systems built an AI model, Larch Forecast, that predicts the weather up to ten days ahead. In tests on two years of past weather, its ten-day forecasts had about 12 per cent fewer errors. The comparison was with numerical weather prediction, the standard method.
explainer.matters: Forecasts guide farmers, airlines and emergency plans. Fewer errors ten days out gives people more time to prepare for storms and heat. A small gain in accuracy reaches many people at once. Weather agencies pay close attention to any method that beats the standard one.
explainer.ai_helped: Larch Weather Systems built Larch Forecast. The model learns from past weather records, so it finds patterns in them instead of solving the equations of the air. The company also helped write the paper. The tests in the paper are the company's own.
explainer.how_sure: Applied. The Meridian Weather Service says it now relies on the model for its daily forecasts. Science published the paper after peer review, and Larch Weather Systems, the maker, helped write it. The tests used past weather only, so live forecasts may differ.
explainer.background: For many years, weather agencies have forecast by solving physical equations on large computers. Tests on past weather show how a new model would have done on days that are already known.
explainer.could_lead: If the gain holds in other seasons and other places, forecasters could trust longer forecasts and warn people earlier. Outside teams may test the model next, on live forecasts and in other regions.

evidence.quote: Larch Forecast is an AI model that predicts weather up to ten days ahead
runs Larch Forecast alongside its own system

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: A robot lab reports a magnetic material that keeps its strength

explainer.found: A robot lab run by an AI planner reported a new magnetic material that keeps its strength up to 400 degrees.
explainer.matters: Strong magnets that work in the heat could help motors and generators, so a new material with that property would be useful.
explainer.ai_helped: Hartwell Materials Lab built the Cobalt Planner, which chose each sample to make next. Robots made and tested the samples.
explainer.how_sure: Checked. Physical Review Letters published the paper after peer review. Hartwell Materials Lab, the maker of the planner, wrote the paper.
explainer.background: A magnet loses strength as it gets hot, and each material has its own limit.
explainer.could_lead: If other labs repeat the result, the material could be tried in real machines.

evidence.quote: The Cobalt Planner, built by Hartwell Materials Lab, chose each sample to make next

rung_history.note: Retracted by Physical Review Letters on 8 Oct 2026.

sources.title: SAMPLE: A robot lab reports a new magnetic material
SAMPLE: Retraction: A robot lab reports a new magnetic material

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: An AI checker flags a gap in a published proof

explainer.found: Marlow Labs says its AI checker, Gapfinder, read a published proof in number theory and flagged a gap in one step.
explainer.matters: Mathematicians rely on checks like this to trust long proofs, so a flagged gap needs a careful answer.
explainer.ai_helped: Marlow Labs built Gapfinder, which found the gap with no human help.
explainer.how_sure: Preprint. arXiv hosts the paper, which has not been peer reviewed. Marlow Labs, the maker of the checker, is the source of the claim.
explainer.background: A published proof is one that a journal has accepted.
explainer.could_lead: If the gap is real, the authors could repair the step or withdraw the proof.

evidence.quote: The checker found the gap with no human help

rung_history.note: Kestrel College says the authors reject the claim and say the flagged step is correct.

sources.title: SAMPLE: Gapfinder checks a published proof and flags a gap
SAMPLE: Authors reply to an AI checker's claim of a gap

ledger_for_sunday.title: SAMPLE: An open dataset of 40,000 AI-run survey interviews

explainer.found: The Coldwater Institute survey lab released 40,000 interviews that an AI interviewer ran by chat with adult volunteers.
explainer.matters: Surveys take a great deal of time. A shared dataset lets other researchers study how AI interviewers work.
explainer.ai_helped: The Coldwater Institute survey lab built Survey Voice, which asked the questions and followed up on answers. People wrote the questions and checked a sample of the transcripts.
explainer.how_sure: Preprint. SSRN hosts the paper, which has not been peer reviewed. The Coldwater Institute survey lab, which built the system, is the source.
explainer.background: Researchers use interviews to learn what people think and why.
explainer.could_lead: AI interviewers could make large surveys cheaper, if their answers match those of people.

evidence.quote: Survey Voice asked the questions and followed up on answers
